notes.2: This question about a falling object was answered correctly by many of the stronger candidates. However, other candidates thought the forces on the accelerating object were balanced.
notes.3: Candidates found this question on determining the resultant velocity challenging. Many weaker candidates did not recognise that the direction of the aircraft was at right angles to the direction of the wind, and therefore just subtracted one speed from the other.
notes.6: Candidates had to recognise that when the cyclist travels at a constant speed, the forces acting on the cyclist must be balanced. Only stronger candidates answered correctly. Other candidates had the misconception that the driving force had to be larger than the frictional force.
notes.8: This was a challenging question on moments with only stronger candidates choosing the correct option. Weaker candidates chose option C as they did not recognise that the perpendicular distance in diagram Q was greater.
notes.9: The strongest candidates were able to identify the correct option. Other candidates multiplied the change in speed by the mass instead of the change in velocity and chose option A.
notes.11: Many weaker candidates had the misconception that nuclei are negatively charged and chose the incorrect option C.
notes.13: For this question, candidates had to read values from the graph and then rearrange an equation for pressure in a liquid to calculate the density of the liquid. Most stronger candidates chose the correct option, but weaker candidates found this challenging.
notes.16: Candidates had to use their knowledge of thermal energy transfer in this question. Only stronger candidates chose the correct answer. Weaker candidates had the misconception that a white car would show a greater rate of temperature decrease.
notes.17: This question assessed candidates’ knowledge of the nature of water waves. Many candidates answered this correctly, but some weaker candidates had the misconception that water waves are longitudinal.
notes.18: Most candidates could identify which lens diagram showed the lens being used as a magnifying glass, with a common incorrect response being option B as it showed an enlarged, but real, image.
notes.22: Most stronger candidates answered this question correctly while weaker candidates chose the incorrect option A because they forgot to halve the time.
notes.23: Candidates had to recall facts about electromagnets in this question. Many candidates answered this correctly, with incorrect answers spread over the other three options.
notes.25: This question assessed candidates’ knowledge of the relationship between the resistance of a wire, its length and its diameter. Only stronger candidates could identify the correct relationship shown by the graph.
notes.26: This question required candidates to use an equation to firstly calculate the energy used by the heater and then the cost. Only stronger candidates answered this correctly with others choosing option B.
notes.27: Candidates were assessed on their knowledge of the effect of changing the length and diameter of a wire on its resistance. Many candidates chose the correct option, but weaker candidates’ responses were evenly distributed across the four options.
notes.30: Only stronger candidates could use the left-hand rule successfully in order to determine the direction of the force on the wire.
notes.31: Candidates were assessed on their knowledge of the construction of a d.c. motor and an a.c. generator. Many candidates answered this correctly, but weaker candidates thought that neither the motor nor the generator contained a magnet.
notes.32: Candidates had to use a transformer equation to determine the voltage across the primary coil and then use this value to calculate the current in the primary coil. This was a challenging question for weaker candidates with few selecting correctly and their answers distributed across the three incorrect options.
notes.33: Candidates had to apply their knowledge of the alpha-particle scattering experiment to draw a conclusion about the observations. Stronger candidates reached the correct conclusion, but the incorrect answers were distributed evenly across the three incorrect options.
notes.35: Few candidates could recall what change occurred in a nucleus during beta emission.
notes.36: In this question, candidates had to work out the half-life of the radioactive isotope using the graph and the background count rate (syllabus statement 5.2.1.5). Stronger candidates answered this correctly. The most common error was not to take the background count rate into account, therefore choosing incorrect option B.
notes.38: For this question, candidates had to recall facts about comets. Although most candidates knew the shape of a comet’s orbit, many candidates had the misconception that the Sun is positioned at the centre of a comet’s orbit.
notes.40: Candidates had to recall which quantity can be determined using the brightness of a supernova in a distant galaxy (syllabus statement 6.2.3.8) and many candidates answered this correctly. However, others had the misconception that the speed at which the galaxy is moving away from the Earth can be determined and therefore chose incorrect option A.
notes.general_comments: Questions on speed–time graphs and power were answered well. There were some misconceptions about resultant forces and the charge on a nucleus. It was evident that questions involving resultant velocity, resultant forces and impulse were not well understood. The questions on the new syllabus topic, space physics, showed a mixed standard of recall and understanding.
